text: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed two bills further curbing artificial intelligence risks for children, leveraging a core campaign policy ahead of New York’s gubernatorial election next week. One measure will impose some of the strictest restrictions in the country on chatbots that interact with children on sensitive topics including mental health policies. Another will require baby monitors with internet connections to have security features blocking outside watchers or listeners. The chatbot measure will take effect in the coming months, and the baby monitor measure will take effect in 90 days, according to Hochul’s office. Hochul (D) made her push to regulate the impacts of technology — including social media restrictions and a school cell phone ban — a key part of her reelection bid. Hochul is facing Republican Bruce Blakeman in a race that an Oct. 28 Siena poll showed her leading by 14 points. Restrictions on children’s online safety have proven a relatively effective way for both Democrats and Republicans around the country to wade into regulating technology in the absence of comprehensive federal standards. Other Big Tech priorities, including artificial intelligence, have been trickier for state officials to navigate. In 2025, Hochul signed one of the strongest bills in the US to force disclosure of critical risks from large AI companies, mirroring similar legislation in California and Illinois. The bills she signed Wednesday will “send a clear message” to companies manufacturing technologically advanced products, including chatbots, Hochul said in a statement. “No company should be peddling chatbots to kids encouraging self-harm or pretending to be their friend or more,” Hochul added. “And no new parent should have to worry that predatory hackers are spying on their new family through their baby monitors.” The chatbot bill, sponsored by Assemblymember Alex Bores (D) and state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D), specifically prohibits companies using AI-powered chatbots from using “unsafe features” for minors, including those that are sexually explict, encourage self-harm, or pretend to be human. It will require companies to verify the ages of their users and gives Democratic state Attorney General Letitia James’ office the power to seek civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation. Child safety advocates, including Common Sense Media, cheered the new laws, but business groups have pushed back on the chatbot bill’s scope. Providing news, analysis, data and opportunity insights.
